analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $20 and makes insulin affordable for uninsured people with diabetes.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up by either committee it was sent to and died at the end of the 116th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Matt's Act would cap what people with diabetes pay out of pocket for insulin under private insurance at $20 per fill — or $0 if they're on a high-deductible plan — and require insurers to cover insulin before any deductible is met. It would also require drug manufacturers to publish the real net price of each insulin drug (what it costs after all the rebates and discounts hidden in today's pricing system), and make pharmacies sell insulin to uninsured people at that published net price plus a small dispensing charge. The bill was introduced in July 2020, referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.3 million insulin-dependent Americans with private insurance would pay at most $20 per fill (free on high-deductible plans) instead of hundreds of dollars when deductibles haven't been met, ending the practice of insulin rationing driven by cost. Uninsured people with diabetes, who currently pay full inflated list prices out of pocket, could buy insulin at the actual net price that manufacturers charge after rebates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users with private insurance or no insurance

how_it_helps.text: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs for people with private insurance at $20, or $0 in high-deductible plans, without regard to deductible.
Requires insulin manufacturers to publish the average net price of each insulin drug quarterly, exposing the gap between list prices and prices after rebates.
Lets uninsured people with diabetes buy insulin at the published net price plus a dispensing charge capped at 10% of net price, instead of the full list price.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would lose revenue from the higher out-of-pocket prices paid by insured patients today and would face public disclosure of their net prices, likely pressuring list prices downward. Health insurers would absorb some cost where $20 caps exceed existing coinsurance, and pharmacies would have to dispense to uninsured people at net price, possibly at a loss on some drugs.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay but does not directly cap what manufacturers can charge insurers, so insurers and employers could face higher premiums to cover the shortfall; some cost-shifts to premiums are possible.

It only applies to private insurance — people on Medicare or Medicaid are not covered by the provision (though they have separate protections), and uninsured people still pay net price plus charges, which is not free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: insulin is an essential drug for survival for people with Type 1 diabetes, and the bill removes the risk of cost-driven rationing. The main cost is absorbed largely by manufacturers and, to a lesser degree, insurers and pharmacies. The bill's design is narrow and avoids broad price controls, focusing only on insulin; the main downside is that insurers might pass some of the cost into premiums.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor committees on introduction, where it stayed without a hearing or vote until the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 22, 2020 by Rep. Jeff Fortenberry with Rep. Angie Craig as cosponsor.
Referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor; neither scheduled action on the bill.
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers avoided having net prices disclosed and rebates exposed to public scrutiny, and insurers avoided the $20 cap. No one benefited from the bill's failure except those whose pricing practices would have been constrained.

sides.party_line_note: Introduced by a Republican with one Democratic cosponsor, but the bill was too narrow to attract wider party organizing and died in committee without action from either party.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: Would have to publish net prices quarterly, exposing how much they discount list prices after rebates, and would lose the out-of-pocket revenue collected from insured patients paying list-price-linked copays. The disclosure requirement is the mechanism most threatening to manufacturers.
The bill requires that net prices include all rebates and concessions PBMs receive, which would expose their role in inflating list prices.
Must cover insulin without regard to deductible and cap patient cost at $20, which could raise plan costs, but insurers also benefit from transparency about manufacturer net prices.
